title: Luther-Emery liquid in one-dimensional attractive Fermi gas
authors: Hai-Ying Cui, Yi-Cong Yu, Aashish Kafle, Han Pu, Randall G. Hulet, Thierry Giamarchi, Xî-Wen Guan
abstract: One-dimensional (1D) interacting Fermi gases underpin a rich variety of quantum liquids, ranging from the Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid and the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov paired state to the Luther-Emery liquid (LEL). Notably, the LEL-characterized by gapless excitations in charge or spin degree of freedom and gapped excitations in the other-has long been theoretically predicted but has eluded definitive experimental observation to date. By exactly solving the attractive Yang-Gaudin model via the Bethe ansatz, we fully determine the low-energy excitation spectra for both spin and charge channels. For fully paired fermions, the spectrum features gapped spin excitation coexisting with gapless charge excitation. We further employ bosonization to derive analytical expressions for the dynamical structure factor (DSF) of the gapped spin excitation, which is a long-standing challenge in this study. In the trapped gas, we find that the spin Bragg spectroscopy peak occurs at a much higher frequency than the charge-mode peak, where the splitting frequency between these two peaks scales approximately linearly with the interaction strength. Crucially, the spin gap manifests as a sharp threshold in the spin DSF, below which spectral weight is completely absent, proving a direct and unambiguous spectroscopic fingerprint of the LEL. Our work establishes quasi-1D trapped attractive Fermi gases as a pristine experimental platform for the long-sought direct observation of the LEL.
summary: This paper analyzes the Luther-Emery liquid phase in 1D attractive Fermi gases by solving the Yang-Gaudin model. It establishes that the LEL is marked by a fundamental dichotomy: gapless charge excitations and gapped spin excitations. This signature is predicted to be observable as a distinct, measurable spectral splitting using Bragg spectroscopy in trapped atomic gases.
main_problem: The primary goal is to theoretically predict and experimentally identify the Luther-Emery liquid (LEL) phase in a one-dimensional attractive Fermi gas, a state that has been predicted but remains experimentally elusive.
main_result: The LEL is characterized by a distinct spectroscopic signature: gapless charge excitations coexisting with gapped spin excitations, which can be unambiguously detected via spin Bragg spectroscopy in trapped gases.
method: The authors combine exact solutions (Bethe ansatz) for the model Hamiltonian with bosonization techniques and the Local Density Approximation (LDA) to analyze both homogeneous and trapped systems.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional (1D) attractive Fermi gas, modeled using the Yang-Gaudin Hamiltonian. The analysis focuses on the fully paired phase, contrasting the gapless charge sector with the gapped spin sector.
key_observables: Dynamical Structure Factors (DSF) for both spin and charge channels, and the frequency splitting between the spin Bragg peak and the charge-mode peak.
important_parameters: Interaction strength, spin polarization ($p$), and the low-momentum behavior of the excitation spectra ($\omega_c \propto |q|$ vs. $\omega_s \ge \omega_{th}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the LDA for trapped systems and assumes the system can be mapped to a free fermion model at specific points (e.g., $K_s = 1/2$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic comparison of gapless charge vs. gapped spin excitations, and show the normalized spin DSF exhibiting a clear vanishing weight below a threshold frequency ($\omega_{th}$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework using the Bethe ansatz and bosonization to deriving the distinct gapless/gapped excitation spectra, culminating in applying these results to predict measurable spectral splitting in trapped gas Bragg spectroscopy.
why_interesting: This work bridges fundamental condensed matter theory (LEL physics) with modern experimental platforms (ultracold atoms), providing a concrete, measurable spectroscopic fingerprint for a complex quantum state.
